Overview of endocrine system
• Different effects of hormones

• Growth and development (E.g. growth hormone)

• Regulation of cellular metabolism (E.g. epinephrine)
• Regulation of body defenses (E.g. Thymosin)

text:
Overview of endocrine system
• “Glands” in human body can be divided into endocrine glands and exocrine glands.
• Endocrine glands: ductless glands that secrete hormones into blood
• Exocrine glands: glands that secrete nonhormone chemicals to a surface through ducts
• Sweat gland, skin sebaceous gland, and gastric gland are examples of exocrine glands.
• Only endocrine glands belong to “endocrine system”.

text:
Hormone Chemical Structure
• Chemical structure of a hormone determines its solubility in water. This is related to:
• How is it transported in blood?
• How does it affect its target cells?
• Two classes:
• (1) Protein or amino acid based Most hormones are proteins or amino acid based. (E.g. LH, Epi, ADH) These are usually water soluble and cannot cross cell membrane.
• (2) Steroids Some hormones are made from cholesterol. (E.g. aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone) These are all lipid soluble and can cross cell membrane.

text:
Mechanisms of Hormone Action
• Hormones are carried by blood to all tissues. However, not all cells are affected by 1 hormone.
• The cells, that are affected, are “target cells” of a certain hormone.
• These cells have specific receptor proteins in cytoplasm or in cell membrane.
• Hormone molecules bind to receptor proteins and trigger a series of changes of these cells.

text:
Mechanisms of Hormone Action
• Mechanisms of water soluble hormones:
• (1) Bind to “plasma membrane receptors” on cell membrane
• (2) Trigger increase of different “second messengers” inside the cell
• Examples of common second messengers include cAMP, calcium ions, cGMP, etc.
• (3) Second messengers activate or inactivate enzymes inside cytoplasm.
• (4) Cellular activities are changed!

text:
Mechanisms of Hormone Action
• Mechanisms of lipid soluble hormones:
• (1) Bind to “intracellular receptors” in cytoplasm or in nucleus
• (2) Hormone-receptor complex binds to a specific DNA region
• (3) A specific mRNA is produced from certain region of DNA.
• (4) The mRNA leaves nucleus and attaches to ribosomes on rough ER.
• (5) New proteins are produced to change cellular activities.

text:
Regulation of Hormone Secretion
• The synthesis and release of most hormones are regulated by some type of negative feedback mechanism.
• 3 types of stimuli trigger endocrine glands to release more hormones.
• (1) Humoral stimuli concentrations of certain molecules (E.g. glucose) or ions (E.g. Calcium ions) in blood
• “Low Na + or high K + blood levels ➔ Adrenal gland secretes more aldosterone ➔ Increase Na + and decrease K +
• (2) Neural stimuli
• “Sympathetic nervous system ➔ Adrenal gland secretes more epinephrine (Epi) ➔ Enhance “Fight-or-flight” responses
• (3) Hormonal stimuli concentrations of other hormones in blood

text:
Regulation of Hormone Secretion
• Hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis
• (1) Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) secreted from hypothalamus stimulate pituitary
• (2) Pituitary secretes more TSH
• (3) Thyroid gland secretes more T3 and T4
• (4) High blood levels of T3 and T4 decrease the secretion of TRH and TSH
• (5) T3 and T4 secretions decrease and blood levels of T3 and T4 are kept within normal range T3
